lines.text:
Fill Up and Move On — The Gas Station as Roadside Infrastructure

A gas station is one of the most purely functional spaces in modern life. You arrive because you must — because the fuel gauge on your dashboard is approaching empty — and you leave as quickly as possible. Yet this unremarkable stop is a surprisingly complex piece of infrastructure, and the vocabulary it teaches is immediately useful for any driver.

The forecourt is covered by a canopy — a flat roof supported by columns that protects customers from rain and sun. A gas pump stands on an island between parking spots. Each pump has a nozzle — the handle-and-spout device that delivers fuel — and a card reader for payment. A price sign displays the cost per litre or gallon. The fuel options are typically unleaded (regular petrol), premium (higher octane), and diesel. The driver opens the fuel cap, selects a fuel grade, inserts the nozzle, and squeezes the handle. A receipt prints when fueling is complete.

Vehicle types rotate through constantly: a car, a truck, an SUV, a van, a motorcycle, a sedan, a convertible, a trailer, and occasionally a bus. Each has different fuel requirements and tank sizes.

The convenience store attached to the station is where margins are made. Fuel is sold at thin profit; the snacks, drinks, coffee, ice, candy, chips, gum, lottery tickets, newspapers, and sunglasses inside generate the real revenue. A cashier operates the register. An ATM provides cash.

Maintenance services are often available. An air pump inflates tyres — checking tire pressure is recommended monthly. Windshield fluid, oil, coolant, antifreeze, and wiper blades are sold on racks. A car wash — automated or hand — occupies one side. A vacuum cleans the interior. A funnel helps pour fluids. A squeegee — a handled rubber blade — cleans the windshield manually. A paper towel dries it.

The supporting infrastructure includes a parking spot, a dumpster for waste, a restroom (often requiring a key from the cashier), an ice machine, a trash can, and a water hose.

The actions performed here are routine: pumping gas, paying, checking oil, filling tires, washing the windshield, fueling, and driving away. An attendant — where full-service stations still exist — performs these tasks for the customer.

Gas stations are evolving. Electric vehicle charging stations are appearing alongside traditional pumps. Some stations now offer coffee bars, fast food, and even co-working spaces. But the core function remains unchanged: energy transfer — converting stored fuel into the motion that keeps society moving.

lines.text: 'Petrol' (British) and 'gasoline/gas' (American) are uncountable — never 'a petrol' or 'a gas.' Use: 'some petrol', 'petrol', 'enough petrol.' Similarly: 'fuel' is uncountable: 'I need fuel' (not *a fuel). 'Diesel' is also uncountable when referring to the fuel: 'This car runs on diesel.'

lines.text: Reported speech with a past reporting verb ('asked') requires tense backshift: 'want' → 'wanted.' Direct: 'Do you want premium or unleaded?' Reported: 'He asked if I wanted...' No backshift needed with present reporting verbs: 'He asks if I want...' Full sequence: will → would, can → could, is → was.

lines.text: 'For' + duration: 'for five hours', 'for three days.' 'Since' + point in time: 'since this morning', 'since 6 a.m.', 'since we left home.' Never *'since five hours.' Present perfect continuous emphasises ongoing duration: 'I've been driving for five hours' = I started five hours ago and I'm still driving.

lines.text: 'Fewer' + countable plural: 'fewer stations', 'fewer pumps', 'fewer attendants.' 'Less' + uncountable: 'less traffic', 'less fuel', 'less congestion.' Gas stations are countable individual locations, so 'fewer' is correct. Remember: if you can count them individually, use 'fewer.'

lines.text: 'Need to be + past participle' (passive): 'needs to be checked.' Or 'need + -ing' (active form with passive meaning): 'The car needs checking.' Never *'needs to be check' — the passive requires the past participle. 'Have something done' (causative): 'have the oil checked' = arrange for someone to check it.

lines.text: 'Petrol' (BrE) = 'gas/gasoline' (AmE). 'Petrol station' (BrE) = 'gas station' (AmE). 'Filling station' and 'service station' are used in both. 'Forecourt' (BrE) = the paved area with the pumps. In the UK, fuel is sold per litre; in the US, per gallon (1 US gallon = 3.785 litres).

lines.text: 'Unleaded' = standard petrol (no lead additive). 'Premium/Super' = higher-octane petrol. 'Diesel' = different fuel for diesel engines (NEVER put petrol in a diesel car or vice versa — it causes serious damage). 'LPG' = liquefied petroleum gas (cheaper, less common).

lines.text: 'Service station' (BrE) or 'rest stop' (AmE) = a larger facility on a motorway with fuel, food, toilets, and sometimes a hotel. UK motorway services (Moto, Welcome Break, Roadchef) are famous for being expensive. Many drivers bring packed food instead.

lines.text: 'Slow charger' = 3-7kW, takes 8-12 hours (home charging). 'Fast charger' = 7-22kW, takes 3-4 hours. 'Rapid charger' = 50-150kW, takes 30-60 minutes. 'Ultra-rapid' = 150-350kW, takes 15-30 minutes. Many petrol stations are adding EV charging points.
